claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by dislocation-based slip avalanches.
Slip avalanches produce abrupt stress drops during high-rate deformation.
Slip events become more pronounced as strain rate increases and temperature decreases.
Higher strain rates and lower temperatures increase yield strength and work-hardening by reducing the time or thermal activation available for dislocation recovery.
As-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn typically has a single-phase or dual-phase microstructure containing FCC and possibly minor BCC constituents.
The initial as-cast microstructure may contain shear-band precursors.
The hypothesis can be tested using controlled uniaxial tension or compression over varied strain rates and temperatures.
The proposed strain-rate range extends from approximately 10^-3 s^-1 to above 10^3 s^-1.
The proposed temperature range extends from cryogenic to moderately elevated temperatures.
Slip avalanches cause localized dislocation-density accumulation and emergent adiabatic shear bands or localized deformation zones.
Competition between dislocation nucleation and recovery or healing produces avalanche-like slip events.
At high strain rate and low temperature, stress-strain curves will show sharper yield points, intermittent stress drops, higher yield strength, and enhanced work-hardening.
At low strain rate or higher temperature, increased dislocation healing will produce more uniform plastic flow.
Quasi-static deformation at moderate temperature provides a baseline with smoother plastic flow and lower yield strength.
The hypothesis is restricted to as-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn that has not undergone substantial annealing, severe plastic deformation, or associated microstructural changes.

The mechanism is falsified if high-rate, low-temperature tests show neither intermittent stress drops nor a significant change in slip-avalanche magnitude or frequency relative to quasi-static conditions.
